notes.meaning: The writer expresses deep love for the place where God lives among His people. He addresses the Lord as the ruler over all the armies of heaven, yet marvels at how lovely and dear His holy tent is. Being away from the sanctuary makes him appreciate its beauty even more.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Latin teaching read the title's reference to winepresses as a symbol of the Church, where believers are pressed by earthly troubles to become wine for God's storehouse.

notes.meaning: A deep ache fills the psalmist's whole body and spirit because he cannot be at God's house. His longing is so intense that he feels faint and worn out. Most of all, he wants real fellowship with the living God Himself, not just the physical courts.

Small birds like sparrows and swallows make their homes right beside God's altars. The writer gently envies these little creatures because they can live and raise their young so close to the place of sacrifice. He calls God his King and Lord, holding tightly to Him in personal trust.

Those who live and serve constantly in God's house are truly happy. The priests and temple workers enjoyed daily closeness to God, and their ongoing duty was to praise Him. Spending life in worship is a joyful and blessed work.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Latin commentary applied this continuous dwelling and praise to the heavenly city, where the saved will spend eternity in an unceasing song of praise.

notes.meaning: True blessing belongs to anyone who relies on God for strength rather than trusting in human power. Even when such people are far from Jerusalem, their hearts are set on the road that leads to worship. Their daily journey is shaped by a deep desire to seek God.

Pilgrims often had to travel through dry, difficult places on their way to the sanctuary. Yet their faith and God's provision turn that barren ground into a place of fresh springs, and autumn rains fill the pools. In the same way, God refreshes His people with spiritual comfort during hard seasons.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient Latin teaching treated the valley of weeping as a picture of earthly suffering, where the tears of faithful believers are received by God like sweet wine.

notes.meaning: Instead of wearing out on the long trek, the travelers gain fresh energy as they go forward. God supplies their needs along the path so they do not faint. Every one of them completes the journey safely and appears before God on Mount Zion.

The writer turns his longing into a direct, urgent cry for God to hear him. He calls on the Lord of Hosts, who rules all heavenly armies, and the God of Jacob, who keeps His covenant promises. He asks to be brought back into God's presence.

The psalmist asks God to look kindly on the leader chosen to protect the nation. In ancient Israel, kings and priests were anointed—marked as holy for God's special service by having oil poured on them. The prayer asks God to defend this leader so the whole community can be blessed.

Spending just one day close to God is far better than a thousand days spent anywhere else. The writer would rather sit at the doorway of God's house doing the humblest job than live in the luxury of wicked homes. True joy is found in being near the Lord, not in earthly honor.

The Lord is compared to a sun because He gives light and life, and to a shield because He guards His people from harm. He freely gives His favor and honor, and He never holds back anything that is truly good from those who walk faithfully before Him.

The psalm ends by celebrating anyone who puts complete trust in the Lord of Hosts. Even if someone cannot physically reach the temple courts, placing wholehearted faith in God brings true safety and lasting happiness.
